lessons.title: Greeting and addressing people politely
lessons.objective: Greet people at different periods of the day, answer greetings and address adults politely.
lessons.course:
We greet with the right words for the time: Good morning (until midday), Good afternoon (after midday), Good evening (when night falls) and Good night (when we go to bed or leave at night).
We address adults politely: Mr Ndi, Mrs Ewane, Uncle, Auntie, Sir, Madam. We answer a greeting with the same greeting and a question: “Good morning, Mrs Ewane. How are you?”

support.title: Practise with the adult
support.text:
Good evening, Uncle Fon. How are you?
I am fine, thank you. And you?

lessons.model: At 7 p.m., Ngum visits her neighbour. She says: “Good evening, Mrs Ewane. How are you?” Mrs Ewane answers: “Good evening, Ngum. I am well, thank you.”
lessons.guided: Look at four clock faces (7 a.m., 2 p.m., 7 p.m., 10 p.m.). For each one, greet an adult with the right greeting and a polite title.
lessons.exercise: It is 3 p.m. You meet your teacher, Mr Tanyi. What do you say?
lessons.remediation: Work first with morning and night, then add afternoon and evening.
lessons.transfer: Greet three adults today with the right greeting and their title.
lessons.materials: Clock faces or pictures of the sun and the moon.

practice.prompt: Match each time with the greeting.
practice.answer: 8 a.m.: Good morning; 2 p.m.: Good afternoon; 7 p.m.: Good evening.
practice.explanation: The greeting changes with the time of day.

practice.prompt: Which greeting do we say when we leave at night to go to bed?
practice.explanation: “Good night” is said when leaving at night or going to bed.

practice.prompt: Listen and answer the greeting politely.
practice.listen: Good morning, Ayuk. How are you?
practice.answer: Good morning, sir. I am fine, thank you. And you?
practice.explanation: Answer the greeting and ask back.

lessons.title: Reading aloud: sight words and long words
lessons.objective: Read sight words and multisyllabic words quickly, then read a short text aloud with good intonation.
lessons.course:
Sight words are words we see very often: the, was, said, they, because, where. We learn to read them at once, without sounding each letter.
Long words can be cut into syllables: ba-ske-ball, bed-room, kit-chen, re-mem-ber. We read each part, then the whole word.
When we read aloud, we stop at full stops and our voice goes up at the end of a question.

support.title: Read aloud
support.text:
Our house has a parlour, a kitchen and two bedrooms.
Where is my brother? He said he was in the garden.

lessons.model: The adult reads the text slowly, stops at each full stop and raises the voice at the question.
lessons.guided: Read the sight words on cards as fast as you can. Clap the syllables of the long words. Then read the short text aloud twice.
lessons.exercise: How many syllables are there in “remember”?
lessons.remediation: Practise five sight words a day; clap long words before reading them.
lessons.transfer: Read a short text from a newspaper, a label or a book aloud to someone at home.
lessons.materials: Sight word cards, a short text.

practice.prompt: Put the syllables in order.
Which word is a sight word we read at once?
How many syllables in “basketball”?

lessons.title: Handwriting: copying a short text in joint script
lessons.objective: Copy a short text of at least five sentences legibly in upright joint script.
lessons.course:
In joint script, the letters of a word are joined by small strokes. We keep letters the same height, we write upright and we leave a space between words.
We copy a whole sentence at a time: we read it, we remember it, we write it, then we check.

support.title: Copy this text
support.text: Our home is small and clean. Mama cooks in the kitchen. Papa repairs the door. My sister sweeps the yard. I water the flowers.

lessons.model: The adult copies the first sentence slowly, joining the letters, and checks each word against the model.
lessons.guided: Copy the five sentences. After each sentence, check: capital letter, spaces, full stop.
lessons.exercise: Copy the first sentence in joint script.
lessons.answer: Our home is small and clean.
lessons.remediation: Copy one sentence a day, joining two letters at a time (ou, me, ll).
lessons.transfer: Copy a short message for your family on a card.

practice.prompt: Copy the five sentences in joint script.
practice.explanation: Check capitals, spaces and full stops.

practice.prompt: What do we leave between two words?
practice.explanation: Spaces make the text easy to read.

practice.prompt: Put the steps of copying in order.
practice.explanation: Copy a whole sentence at a time.

lessons.title: Kinds of nouns, plurals and articles
lessons.objective: Identify common, proper and concrete nouns, form plurals with s, es and ies, and use a, an and the.
lessons.course:
A common noun names any person, place or thing: house, mother, town. A proper noun names a particular one and starts with a capital letter: Bamenda, Mrs Ewane, River Sanaga. A concrete noun names something we can see or touch: a chair, a pot.
Plurals: most nouns add s (room → rooms); nouns ending in s, sh, ch, x add es (box → boxes, dish → dishes); a consonant + y becomes ies (baby → babies).
Articles are noun signals: a before a consonant sound (a bed), an before a vowel sound (an orange), the for a particular thing (the kitchen).
lessons.model: The adult sorts word cards: “Kumba” is proper (capital K); “pot” is common and concrete; “dish” becomes “dishes”.
lessons.guided: Sort ten nouns from the home into common or proper. Then write the plural of each common noun.
lessons.remediation: Practise s plurals first, then es, then ies.
lessons.transfer: Write five things in your home with a or an.

practice.prompt: Complete with the plural.
practice.text: one box, two [[boxes]]; one baby, three [[babies]]; one room, four [[rooms]]
practice.explanation: es after x; y becomes ies; s for most nouns.

practice.prompt: Which one is a proper noun?
practice.explanation: Limbe is the name of a particular town: it starts with a capital letter.

practice.prompt: Complete with a or an.
practice.answer: an orange, a mat, an umbrella.

lessons.title: The universal set and subsets at home
lessons.objective: Describe a universal set and its subsets, and use the symbols { } and ⊂.
lessons.course:
The universal set (U) contains all the things we are talking about. U = {things in our kitchen}.
A subset is a smaller set inside it: {pots} ⊂ U, {spoons} ⊂ U. We list elements between curly brackets and separate them with commas: {pot, plate, cup}.
lessons.model: The adult says: U = {Mama, Papa, Bih, Ayuk, Grandma}. The subset of children is {Bih, Ayuk}.
lessons.guided: Make a universal set with ten objects from the house. Form two subsets and write them with curly brackets.
lessons.exercise: U = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. Write the subset of even numbers.
lessons.remediation: Use real objects in a big ring and small rings inside it.
lessons.transfer: Arrange your belongings in subsets: books, clothes, shoes.
lessons.materials: Objects from the house, strings to make rings.

practice.prompt: U = {mango, orange, carrot, banana, cabbage}. How many elements are in the subset of fruits?
Which symbol means “is a subset of”?
practice.explanation: {pots} ⊂ U means the set of pots is inside U.

practice.prompt: Match each element with its subset.
practice.answer: bed: bedroom; pot: kitchen; sofa: parlour.
practice.explanation: Each element belongs to a subset.

lessons.title: Numbers up to 500: reading, writing, counting
lessons.objective: Count, read and write numbers up to 500, forward and backward.
lessons.course:
We count in ones, tens and hundreds: 198, 199, 200, 201… or 250, 260, 270… or 100, 200, 300, 400, 500.
A number up to 500 has hundreds, tens and units: 384 = 3 hundreds, 8 tens, 4 units.
lessons.model: The adult counts the bags of cement in a store by hundreds and tens: “Three hundred and forty bags.”
lessons.guided: Count on and back from a given number: from 296 to 305, from 480 back to 470.
lessons.remediation: Count in tens up to 100, then in hundreds up to 500.
lessons.transfer: Count the pages of a big book in tens.
lessons.materials: Number cards, bundles of sticks (hundreds, tens, units).

practice.prompt: Which number comes just before 300?
Complete the count in tens.
Put the numbers in order from smallest to biggest.

lessons.title: Place value: thousands, hundreds, tens and units
lessons.objective: Give the place value of each digit in a number and partition numbers.
lessons.course:
In 4 372: 4 is in the thousands place (4 000), 3 in the hundreds place (300), 7 in the tens place (70), 2 in the units place (2).
We can partition: 372 = 300 + 70 + 2.
lessons.model: The adult writes 265 in a table Th | H | T | U and says the value of each digit.
lessons.guided: Write five numbers in the place value table and partition each one.
lessons.exercise: What is the value of 6 in 462?
lessons.remediation: Use bundles of 100, 10 and single sticks.
lessons.transfer: Look at a price (for example 350 frs) and say the value of each digit.
lessons.materials: Place value table, bundles of sticks.

practice.prompt: What is the value of 3 in 3 418?
Complete.
Which number has 2 hundreds, 0 tens and 9 units?

lessons.title: Measuring length: mm, cm, dm, m
lessons.objective: Measure and compare lengths using mm, cm, dm and m, and convert between them.
lessons.course:
We measure length with a ruler or a tape measure. 1 cm = 10 mm; 1 dm = 10 cm; 1 m = 100 cm.
Small things: in mm or cm (a pencil: 15 cm). Big things: in m (a room: 4 m).
lessons.model: The adult measures a table: 1 m and 20 cm, that is 120 cm.
lessons.guided: Measure five objects at home with a ruler or a tape. Write each length in cm, then in m and cm when it is longer than 1 m.
lessons.exercise: How many centimetres are in 1 metre?
lessons.remediation: Measure with a ruler only, in cm.
lessons.transfer: Measure the length of your bed with a tape measure.

practice.prompt: 2 m = ? cm
3 cm = ? mm
Which unit is best to measure the length of a classroom?
practice.explanation: A classroom is long: we use metres.

lessons.title: Our skeleton and our bones
lessons.objective: Identify the main bones of the human skeleton, say what the skeleton does and how to keep bones healthy.
lessons.course:
The skeleton is the frame of the body. It holds us up, protects soft organs and helps us move with the muscles. The skull protects the brain; the ribs protect the heart and lungs; the backbone (spine) holds us upright; the long bones of the arms and legs help us move.
To keep bones strong: eat foods with calcium (milk, fish with bones, green leaves), play and exercise, sit and carry loads correctly.
lessons.model: The adult touches parts of the body: “Here is the skull. Here are the ribs. Feel the backbone down your back.”
lessons.guided: Feel your own bones: skull, jaw, ribs, backbone, knee. Draw a simple skeleton and label five bones.
lessons.exercise: Which bones protect the heart and the lungs?
lessons.remediation: Work with three bones first: skull, ribs, backbone.
lessons.transfer: Show your family how to sit straight and carry a bag on both shoulders.
lessons.materials: A picture of the skeleton, paper, pencils.

practice.prompt: Match each bone with what it protects or does.
practice.answer: skull: brain; ribs: heart and lungs; backbone: upright.

practice.prompt: Which food helps build strong bones?
Draw a simple skeleton and label five bones.
practice.answer: A skeleton with five labelled bones.
practice.explanation: Skull, ribs, backbone, arm bone, leg bone.

lessons.title: J’habite à… Il s’appelle…
lessons.objective: Se présenter et présenter quelqu’un : nom, lieu d’habitation, profession.
lessons.course:
Pour se présenter : « Je m’appelle Ayuk. J’habite à Kumba. » (I live in Kumba.)
Pour présenter quelqu’un : « Il s’appelle Ndi. Il habite à Bafoussam. Il est menuisier. » / « Elle s’appelle Bih. Elle est infirmière. »

support.title: Dis avec l’adulte
support.text:
Je m’appelle … J’habite à …
Il s’appelle … Il est cultivateur.
Elle s’appelle … Elle est commerçante.

lessons.model: Ngum présente sa famille : « Voici mon père. Il s’appelle Fon. Il habite à Bamenda. Il est chauffeur. »
lessons.guided: Présente-toi, puis présente deux membres de ta famille avec leur ville et leur métier.
lessons.remediation: Commence par « Je m’appelle » et « J’habite à », puis passe à « il » et « elle ».
lessons.transfer: Présente un voisin en français à ta famille.

practice.prompt: Complète.
practice.text: Je m’[[appelle]] Bih. J’[[habite]] à Limbé.
practice.answer: Je m’appelle Bih. J’habite à Limbé.

practice.prompt: Relie la personne à la bonne phrase.
practice.answer: Il pour un garçon ; Elle pour une fille.

practice.prompt: Écoute et répète.
practice.listen: Je m’appelle Enow. J’habite à Buea. Mon père est infirmier.
practice.answer: Je m’appelle Enow. J’habite à Buea. Mon père est infirmier.

lessons.title: Our family history: time and sources
lessons.objective: Use the notion of time (past, present, future) and identify sources of history in the family.
lessons.course:
History studies the past. We place events in time: long ago, last year, today, next year. A timeline shows events in order.
Sources of history tell us about the past: elders’ stories (oral sources), old photos and letters (written and picture sources), old objects (a grinding stone, a calabash).
lessons.model: Grandfather shows an old photo of the family compound and tells how it looked when he was young.
lessons.guided: Ask an elder three questions about the past. Make a family timeline with five events (births, moves, school).
lessons.exercise: Name one source of history in a family.
lessons.answer: For example: an old photo or an elder’s story.
lessons.remediation: Order three events of your own life first.
lessons.transfer: Keep an old object or photo with its story written on a card.
lessons.materials: Old photos or objects (with permission), paper.

practice.prompt: Put the events of Ayuk’s life in order.
practice.explanation: A timeline shows the order of events.

practice.prompt: An elder tells about the old market. What kind of source is it?
Draw your family timeline with five events.
practice.answer: A timeline with five events in order.
practice.explanation: Put the oldest event on the left.

lessons.title: Keeping the house clean: rooms and tools
lessons.objective: Name the sections of the house, the cleaning equipment and keep the house clean.
lessons.course:
A house has sections: the sitting room (parlour), the kitchen, the bedrooms, the veranda and the toilet. Each has its furniture and its equipment.
Cleaning equipment: broom, mop, bucket, dustpan, duster, brush. We sweep, dust, wash and air the rooms, and we put things back in their place.
lessons.model: On Saturday morning, the family cleans: Ayuk sweeps the veranda, Bih dusts the parlour, Papa washes the toilet.
lessons.guided: Make a cleaning rota for the family. Do one task and say which tools you used.
lessons.exercise: Which tool do we use to sweep?
lessons.remediation: Match three rooms with their furniture first.
lessons.transfer: Keep your own room tidy for a week.

practice.prompt: Match each room with something we find in it.
practice.answer: kitchen: stove; bedroom: bed; parlour: chairs.

practice.prompt: Put the cleaning in a good order.
Which tool picks up dirt after sweeping?

lessons.title: Painting my body: colour combinations
lessons.objective: Identify painting materials and paint using appropriate colour combinations.
lessons.course:
Painting materials: brushes, paints, water, a palette, paper or cloth, a rag.
The primary colours are red, yellow and blue. When we mix two of them we get a new colour: red + yellow = orange; yellow + blue = green; blue + red = purple. To paint skin tones we can mix brown with a little white or yellow.
lessons.model: The adult mixes yellow and blue on a palette: “Look, it becomes green.”
lessons.guided: Mix the three secondary colours on a palette. Paint a portrait of yourself with colours you mixed.
lessons.exercise: Which colour do we get with yellow and blue?
lessons.remediation: Mix only two colours at a time with a little paint.
lessons.transfer: Show your family how to make orange from two colours.
lessons.materials: Paints (or coloured chalk), brushes, palette, water, paper.

practice.prompt: Match each mix with its colour.
practice.explanation: Two primary colours make a secondary colour.

practice.prompt: Which one is a primary colour?
practice.explanation: The primary colours are red, yellow and blue.

practice.prompt: Paint or draw your portrait with mixed colours.

lessons.title: Balancing and warm-up exercises
lessons.objective: Balance on one foot and do simple calisthenics safely.
lessons.course:
Before sport, we warm up: we walk, jog slowly, turn the arms and the neck gently. Calisthenics are exercises with our own body: jumping jacks, squats, arm circles.
To balance: fix your eyes on a point, keep your arms open, lift one foot and count slowly to ten.
lessons.model: The adult shows ten jumping jacks, then stands on one foot with open arms for ten seconds.
lessons.guided: Warm up for three minutes. Do ten jumping jacks and ten squats. Balance on each foot for ten seconds.
lessons.exercise: What do we do before sport?
lessons.remediation: Balance with one hand on a wall first.
lessons.transfer: Do the warm-up with your family every morning for a week.
lessons.materials: Open space, a watch or counting.

practice.prompt: Put the warm-up in order.
How many seconds do you count when balancing on one foot?
What helps us balance?
choices: fixing the eyes on a point
practice.answer: fixing the eyes on a point

lessons.title: My language and the languages around me
lessons.objective: Name your language and identify other languages spoken in the community.
lessons.course:
Each family has one or more languages. Cameroon has more than two hundred national languages, plus English and French. In one town or subdivision, several languages are spoken.
We respect all languages and can learn greetings in many of them.
lessons.model: The adult says: “At home we speak our language. Our neighbours speak another one. At school we speak English and French.”
lessons.guided: Ask three people the name of their language. Make a list of the languages of your quarter.
lessons.exercise: Name the language of your family.
lessons.answer: For example: the name of your family language.
lessons.remediation: Ask a parent or an elder the name of the language.
lessons.transfer: Learn to say “good morning” in a language of a neighbour.

practice.prompt: Which languages are official in Cameroon?
Write the names of the languages spoken in your quarter.
How should we treat other languages?

lessons.title: Parts of a computer and what they do
lessons.objective: Describe the role of each component of a computer: keyboard, mouse, monitor, printer, scanner, speakers, microphone.
lessons.course: A computer has input devices (we put information in): keyboard, mouse, microphone, scanner. It has output devices (information comes out): monitor (screen), printer, speakers. The system unit is the “brain” that works on the information. External drives (USB keys) keep files.
lessons.model: The adult points: “I type on the keyboard (input). The text appears on the monitor (output). The printer gives it on paper.”
lessons.guided: Sort pictures of devices into input and output. Draw a computer and label five parts.
lessons.exercise: Is the printer an input or an output device?
lessons.remediation: Learn two input and two output devices first.
lessons.transfer: Name the computer parts you see in a cyber café or an office.
lessons.materials: Pictures of computer parts, or a real computer with an adult.

practice.prompt: Match each device with its role.
practice.answer: keyboard: type; monitor: show; speakers: sound.

practice.prompt: Which one is an input device?
Draw a computer and label five parts.
practice.answer: A labelled drawing of a computer.
practice.explanation: Monitor, keyboard, mouse, system unit, speakers.
